Section IIIA, Empirical Strategy for the administration reform
Section IIIB, Results of the administration reform

observations.statement: Names the tax administration analysis a matched difference-in-differences design and states the estimand as the effect of being assigned to a medium taxpayer office on taxpayer outcomes, later contrasted with a separate tax-rate elasticity estimand.

States that the original assignment formula and worksheets used to place taxpayers into the medium taxpayer offices were not archived, so assignment cannot be reconstructed, and explains that entropy-balancing matching on preperiod size variables is used instead to address the resulting selection concern.

Explicitly explains why a regression discontinuity design is not used for the administration reform: the exact assignment formula is unknown and no sharp discontinuity in assignment probability is observed in the data.

States the elasticity of taxable income estimand with respect to the net-of-tax rate and argues the instrument is valid because it is built by applying the post-reform tax schedule to preperiod firm characteristics, isolating variation from the schedule change rather than contemporaneous behavior.

Describes an instrumental-variables version of the administration treatment regression, used alongside a reduced-form specification, to adjust the reduced-form assignment effect for later crossover of some comparison taxpayers into the treated group.
observations.locator: Section IIIA, equation for the IV specification

observations.statement: Describes the analysis sample as anonymized administrative microdata on corporate taxpayers in regions where a medium taxpayer office was ever created, covering a multi-year panel of tax and payment records drawn from several distinct government data extracts named individually.

Restricts the main administration analysis to regions where offices opened in a single later wave rather than the earlier pilot regions, justified because primary tax offices in the pilot regions had not yet been reorganized to the same administrative structure, which would confound the comparison.
observations.locator: Section IIIA, discussion of office waves

observations.statement: Imposes a common support restriction that drops taxpayers in the extreme tails of the matching-variable distributions on both sides, stating that this excludes very large treated firms and very small comparison firms.

Notes that the largest and most identifiable taxpayers, served by the national large-taxpayer office and by special sector offices, could not be shared with the researchers for anonymity reasons and are therefore excluded from the analysis sample entirely.

Excludes taxpayers reporting zero taxable income from the main elasticity sample, described as standard practice in the literature, and separately examines the extensive-margin decision to move from zero to positive taxable income.

Defines outcome variables from separate administrative sources, namely treasury payment records, the annual income tax return form, and employment withholding forms, and deflates monetary outcomes to a constant base year using a national GDP deflator.

Constructs taxpayer-level balancing weights through an entropy-balancing procedure that matches treated and comparison taxpayers on preperiod gross income, tax paid, and region, choosing the reweighting of the comparison group that minimally departs from uniform weights while equalizing these covariate means.

Constructs the tax-rate-change instrument by applying the post-reform statutory schedule to each taxpayer's preperiod gross and taxable income, so the predicted rate change reflects only the mechanical schedule change rather than the taxpayer's own reporting response.
Specifies the elasticity regression in first-differenced logs of taxable income and of the net-of-tax rate, with base-year log taxable income and log gross income entered as additional controls.

Reports, for each outcome row in the main administration table, the observation count, preperiod weighted means of the treated and comparison groups, and a constructed posttreatment counterfactual mean, alongside the reduced-form and instrumented treatment estimates.

Lists taxpayer and year fixed-effect indicators as explicit rows in the enforcement-slope tables and states the standard-error type and clustering level in the table notes rather than in the column headers.

Reports taxpayer and year fixed-effect indicator rows and observation counts directly in the elasticity table, with the first-stage coefficient and its F-statistic shown in a separate panel above the second-stage estimates.

Does not report R-squared or a mean-of-dependent-variable row on the main regression tables; instead the tables report preperiod weighted means and a constructed posttreatment counterfactual mean as the benchmark for magnitude.

States that standard errors are clustered at the taxpayer level in the main administration and elasticity regressions without giving an explicit econometric rationale for that choice beyond later showing robustness to alternative clustering levels.
observations.quote: Standard errors are clustered by taxpayer.

observations.statement: Uses heteroskedasticity-robust standard errors rather than clustering for the cross-sectional enforcement-slope regressions, in contrast to clustering at the taxpayer level used in the panel difference-in-differences specifications.

Reports, as a robustness exercise rather than as part of the main inference discussion, that results are similar when standard errors are clustered at a taxpayer's originating tax office or at the region instead of at the taxpayer level.
observations.locator: Section IIIA, footnote referencing appendix table

observations.statement: Reports a first-stage F-statistic for the administration-assignment instrument directly in the text and shows the year-by-year first-stage relationship in a figure with confidence bands.
Reports a very large first-stage F-statistic for the tax-schedule instrument in the elasticity analysis, presented in a dedicated first-stage panel above the second-stage estimates in the same table.

Shows year-by-year event-study estimates of the administration treatment effect with confidence bands to visually assess whether treated and comparison taxpayers were on similar trends before the reform, describing the preperiod pattern as flat.

Presents preperiod weighted means for treated and comparison taxpayers not only on the variables explicitly targeted by matching but also on related subcomponents, to argue that balance extends beyond the matched variables themselves.

Reports a density-based check for strategic bunching of taxpayers around the assignment margin and states that no bunching is found in either the pre- or post-reform period, with the supporting figure held in the online appendix.
observations.locator: Section IIIB, footnote referencing appendix figure

observations.statement: Constructs a placebo assignment among comparison taxpayers that mimics the increasing relationship between assignment probability and preperiod size, reruns the main procedure on this placebo treatment, and presents the estimates in an online appendix figure.
observations.quote: no treatment effects for placebo firms

observations.statement: Summarizes robustness of the administration treatment effect to alternative weighting strategies, including no weights, logit and random-forest propensity scores, and inverse-propensity weighting, discussed in a paragraph in the main text with results collected in one appendix table.

Reports that including all administration-office openings, not only the single wave used in the main specification, and adjusting the instrument to allow region-specific timing yields qualitatively similar results, with the estimates and an event-study figure placed in the appendix.

Summarizes elasticity robustness across many alternative specifications, including unweighted estimation, restricting to taxpayers with continuously positive taxable income, using lagged instruments, dropping taxpayer fixed effects in favor of sector fixed effects, and using only one of the two rate-schedule changes, collected in a single large appendix table.

Checks whether the elasticity estimate is driven by taxpayers predicted to receive a rate cut versus those predicted to receive a rate increase, splitting the sample by predicted direction and reporting an event-study figure for this split in the appendix.

Estimates the tax elasticity separately for taxpayers in the higher-enforcement office versus the regular office, using the same balancing weights, to test whether administrative intensity changes behavioral responsiveness to tax rates, and reports a formal test of the difference between the two subsamples.

Reports heterogeneous administration treatment effects by taxpayers' baseline taxable income in an appendix table, used to motivate the assumptions behind extrapolating the estimated effect to taxpayers outside the estimation sample.
observations.locator: Section IIIB, footnote referencing appendix table

observations.statement: Investigates which channel drives the administration effect on tax due by decomposing the response into reported revenue, reported costs, and the collection rate, concluding the pattern is more consistent with previously unreported business activity being reported than with tighter deduction scrutiny or improved collection of amounts already due.
observations.locator: Section IIIB, Mechanisms subsection and Table 1 panels B and C

observations.statement: Tests the model-derived prediction that intensified administration flattens the relationship between enforcement actions and firm size by nonparametrically plotting audit and assessment-letter probabilities against firm size separately for each office type, then formalizing the comparison in regression form.
observations.locator: Section IIIC, Figure 7 and Tables 4 and 5

observations.statement: Cites an outside survey finding higher reported taxpayer satisfaction with the higher-enforcement office than the regular office as suggestive evidence of a compliance-cost channel, while noting that the original survey microdata were not retained.

Benchmarks the administration treatment effect against a constructed counterfactual mean for treated taxpayers, computed by subtracting the estimated effect from realized posttreatment outcomes, following an approach adapted from an earlier labor-economics evaluation study.

Situates the estimated elasticity of taxable income against prior country-specific estimates from developed and developing economies, discussing differences in firm size and in the tax base underlying the compared estimates.

Combines the two estimated policy parameters into a counterfactual calculation of how much the statutory tax rate would have needed to rise to generate the same revenue as the administrative reform, presenting the comparison both under the estimated elasticity and under a zero-elasticity bound.

Computes a ratio of net revenue gained to additional administrative cost for the reform and contrasts this cost-effectiveness with a tax-administration intervention studied in a different country's context.

States as a limitation that the precise taxpayer-assignment formula and files were not retained, which rules out a sharper regression-discontinuity approach and requires relying on a matching-based comparison instead.

Notes that because the administrative data are anonymized, they cannot be linked to external survey or other datasets, limiting the ability to study outcomes beyond what is recorded in the tax administration's own systems.

Acknowledges that scaling the estimated administration effect to taxpayers outside the common-support estimation sample relies on informal upper- and lower-bound assumptions rather than a point-identified extrapolation method.

Cautions that conclusions about how enforcement intensity interacts with firm size may not extend to the very largest taxpayers served by the national large-taxpayer office, which lies outside the estimation sample, because the enforcement-size relationship may already be flat for those firms.
observations.quote: the derivative of enforcement with respect to firm size may already be low

observations.statement: Uses event-study style figures with shaded confidence bands for year-by-year treatment and first-stage estimates, with each figure's notes stating the weighting scheme, the outcome construction, and the level at which standard errors are clustered.
Presents enforcement probabilities as smoothed nonparametric curves against log firm size, separately by office type, with kernel bandwidths stated in the figure notes rather than in the main text.

Reports standard errors in parentheses beneath coefficients without significance stars throughout the main tables, relying on the reported standard errors and surrounding text discussion rather than star thresholds to convey precision.

Previews the main quantitative comparisons from both empirical exercises in the introduction before presenting either analysis in full, and closes the introduction with paragraphs situating the paper in prior literature followed by an explicit roadmap of the remaining sections.

Places a fully worked theoretical model of firm evasion and enforcement before either empirical section, and uses the model's predictions to motivate which outcomes and mechanisms are tested empirically later in the paper.

Embeds most robustness checks as short paragraphs at the end of each results subsection rather than in a separately labeled robustness section, with the great majority of supporting tables and figures held in an online appendix not included in this text.

Lists a formal replication-data citation with a persistent identifier in the reference list, but the article text itself does not contain a dedicated data-and-code availability statement describing what the package contains or how to access it.

Describes the underlying tax microdata as obtained through a government partnership and anonymized under domestic regulation before being shared with the research team, characterizing access as restricted rather than public-use.

concordance.paper_says: Frames the administration analysis primarily as a matched difference-in-differences design (reduced-form equation), with an instrumental-variables version used only to adjust for later crossover of comparison taxpayers into the treated group, not as the primary identification strategy.
concordance.card_shows: Designs d1 and d2 are both recorded with method 'iv' only, extracted from ivreghdfe calls with an endogenous MTO status variable; the card's method vocabulary includes 'did' and 'matching' but neither is used to label these designs.
concordance.note: Both descriptions are technically compatible (the code literally runs 2SLS), but the card's method label omits the difference-in-differences/matching framing that the paper treats as primary.

concordance.paper_says: States that the administration regressions include taxpayer fixed effects and year fixed effects.
concordance.card_shows: spec s1 records fixed_effects as the Stata absorb() variables 'npwp' and 'year', where npwp is the Indonesian taxpayer identification number.

concordance.paper_says: States that standard errors in the administration regressions are clustered at the taxpayer level.
concordance.card_shows: spec s1's se.cluster_level is null; the underlying call uses cluster(`clust'), a Stata local macro whose value was not resolved during code reading.

concordance.paper_says: States that the administration regressions are weighted by taxpayer-specific entropy-balancing weights constructed from 2005 gross income and total taxes paid.
concordance.card_shows: spec s1's structured weights field is null, though the raw formula_or_call string shows a probability weight, [pw=`weight'], confirming a weighting scheme is used without identifying which one.

concordance.paper_says: Describes the comparison group as taxpayers not assigned to the medium taxpayer office, entropy-balanced on 2005 gross income, taxes paid, and region within a common support restriction.
concordance.card_shows: spec s1's comparison_group field is null.

concordance.paper_says: Describes a two-equation instrumental-variables procedure: a first-stage equation predicting the change in marginal tax rate using a schedule-based instrument, and a second-stage equation estimating the elasticity of taxable income.
concordance.card_shows: spec s3 records estimator '2sls', command 'ivreghdfe', with the endogenous regressor and instrument matching the paper's rate-change variable and predicted rate-change instrument.

concordance.paper_says: States that the elasticity regression includes taxpayer and year fixed effects.
concordance.card_shows: spec s3 records fixed_effects as 'year' and 'npwp' (taxpayer identification number), read directly from the absorb() clause.

concordance.paper_says: States that standard errors in the elasticity regression are clustered at the taxpayer level.
concordance.card_shows: spec s3 records se.type 'cluster' and se.cluster_level ['npwp'], where npwp is the taxpayer identification number, read directly from the cluster() clause.

concordance.paper_says: States the elasticity sample uses CIT filings for the tax years immediately surrounding the rate reform, restricted to the same taxpayers as the administration analysis and excluding taxpayers with zero taxable income.
concordance.card_shows: spec s3's sample field is null, though the raw formula_or_call includes an if-condition restricting to a bounded year range and a 'mainsamp' indicator, consistent with an unresolved sample restriction.

concordance.paper_says: Reports first-stage F-statistics for both instrumented regressions directly in the main text and tables, describing both as very strong.
concordance.card_shows: diagnostic x1 records kind 'first_stage' for design d1 with status 'unknown', no observation value, and a note that it was to be extracted from Stata's e(first) but was not resolved during code reading.

concordance.paper_says: Describes extensive robustness checks for both empirical exercises (alternative weighting schemes, common support restrictions, clustering levels, sample definitions, and instrument construction), summarized in main-text paragraphs with detail in the online appendix.
concordance.card_shows: The card's top-level robustness array is empty.

concordance.paper_says: Names several distinct anonymized administrative data extracts obtained from the tax authority (payment, filing, employment withholding, audit, and assessment records) as the data sources.
concordance.card_shows: The card's top-level data array is empty.

gaps: No pre-analysis plan, IRB approval, or participant consent statement appears anywhere in the article text.
No explicit software name (e.g., Stata) appears anywhere in the article text, even though this is a code-based empirical paper.

No dedicated data-and-code availability statement appears in the article body describing what the cited replication package contains or how restricted data can be accessed; only a bibliographic citation of the replication data appears in the reference list.
No explicit multiple-testing adjustment is discussed despite many outcomes and subgroups being tested across the administration tables.
No R-squared or adjusted R-squared is reported on any main regression table.
No explicit justification is given in the main text for choosing the taxpayer level for standard-error clustering, beyond a footnote showing robustness to alternative levels.

reading.note: All 45 pages of the extracted text were read: abstract and introduction, institutional setting and data, the full theoretical model (Section II), both empirical strategy and results sections (III and IV), the conclusion, and the reference list. This text file contains only the published article; the online appendix referenced dozens of times throughout (additional tables, figures, and the generalized model in online Appendix B) is not part of this extracted text and was not read, so appendix-only claims are recorded as basis stated with tags in_appendix and online_appendix_not_available.
